doc.title: Robert Glasper interviewed by Greg Thomas, Clinton, New York, February 20, 2016

title: Mentoring and a school he wants to open
summary: He has no time to mentor, has a 7-year-old son, and wants a school that avoids producing narrow jazz robots.

story.theme_name: Meeting, marrying and raising a family
story.community_name: Talking about my children and grandchildren

blocks.x: Now by the way, you may have noticed you don’t hear yourself in the mic. Just go right ahead.
My name is [sounds like] Johnny Enoch. My question is —
Enoch? I have a song called “Enoch’s Meditation.”
Yes, and I love it. I really do, I love it. My question is do you, or do you have a staff, are you mentoring any other people who would like to be in the industry or in the music?

I don’t have time at the moment. I do have like, you know, if cats come to New York and I’m in New York and I’m doing something I have a few younger cats that they want to come through and hang out and check it out, they can do that periodically here and there. But I haven’t done an actual like mentor thing yet, like hard core. Because I’m just all over the place. And I even tried to give lessons for a year and that didn’t work out. Because just my schedule was too crazy and I have a 7-year-old son myself. So when I’m not crazy he gets all my — he’s here. You know. Yeah, Robbie’s here. He gets all my attention and I don’t have time for another one. But eventually I want to open up a school of some sort that has teachers that are like-minded like me and use that. Because the tools that I have and a lot of my friends have, musician friends have, is something that can sustain a musician in today’s times. You know what I mean? A lot of times colleges put out these like jazz robots. And people say, “well I’m broke” because they don’t know any other kind of music. Can’t play any other kind of music.
Well it used to be where cats would play a jazz gig or a blues gig or R&B, a bar mitzvah.

Yeah. That was the thing. That was what it is. Blues, all that. All that, you remember? One of my favorite musicians was boogie-woogie playing, Mulgrew [Miller] was, all that, you know, Coltrane walking the bars.
